description:
Daniel : Computer Engineering graduate from Costa Rica with knowledge of AI, automation, blockchain, and data analysis. Looking for developers and designers to build something useful together!

Felipe: AI Engineering student in Costa Rica who loves creating things. Always learning and building side projects. Trilingual. Looking for teammates who want to create something real.
summary:
A farmer who rents or buys a plot usually sees it once, on one day. But land changes all year. How much rain falls in October? Does the ground stay bare in the dry months? How steep is it, and what is the soil made of? Most people sign without knowing.

That information is already public. NASA and other agencies publish it for free, but it sits in separate portals made for specialists.

Before the Seed puts it in one place. You mark your plot with coordinates or by drawing it on a map, and in about a minute you get one report: rainfall from GPM IMERG, vegetation over several years from Landsat 8 and 9, elevation and slope from SRTM, soil from SoilGrids and temperature from NASA POWER. Each figure says where it comes from, what period it covers and how big its pixel is, so nobody mistakes a regional average for a measurement of their own field.

An AI assistant then explains the report in plain language and answers questions. It only works with the numbers in the report, and any answer with a figure that is not there gets thrown out. Everything downloads as a PDF.

Before planting, you can compare three crop rotations: the one you use now and two alternatives. For each, the app shows what a published Costa Rican study on beans found about the previous crop, and how exposed the soil would be to rain month by month.

We built it with small farmers in northern Costa Rica in mind, in English and Spanish. It works wherever the data reaches.
details:
You give Before the Seed a location: type the coordinates, search for a town or tap the map, then pick a square around the point or draw the outline of the plot. The server asks five open data services about that area and puts the answers on one page. You see rainfall month by month, how green the plot has been over several years, its elevation and slope, what the soil is made of and the temperature of the region.

Each card says which product the figure comes from, the period it covers, the size of its pixel and whether it describes your plot or the region around it. That last part matters. Landsat sees 30 meters, but the rainfall pixel is about 11 km wide, and we did not want anyone to read a regional average as a measurement of their own field. If one source fails, the others still show up and you can retry the missing one.

A language model then writes a short reading of the results: what looks favourable, what could be a problem and what is worth checking on the ground. You can ask for recommendations, each with its reason, and ask follow-up questions in a chat. The whole report downloads as a PDF.

The last step is for planting. You enter the rotation you use today and two alternatives, and the app shows two things for each one. The first is what a published Costa Rican study found about bean disease depending on the crop grown before. The second is how exposed the soil would be to rain in each month, using the plot's own rainfall and the ground cover you declare. We keep the two readings apart because adding them into one score would hide more than it shows.

Benefits and intended impact

Renting or buying a plot is a decision people make once and pay for over years, and they usually make it after seeing the land on a single day. The data that shows the rest of the year is free, but getting it means several portals, file formats and vocabulary that most farmers have no reason to learn. We want a farmer or an extension worker to get that picture in about a minute, from a phone, without an account.

We showed the project to Oscar Arias Moreira, president of the Chamber of Farmers of Costa Rica. He told us he found it a good and useful idea for the country's agricultural sector and its farmers, and he wants to see the final result and how the project continues.

Tools

It is a web app written in TypeScript with Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel. Leaflet draws the map, geotiff.js reads the soil maps, pdf-lib builds the report and Vitest runs the tests. The texts inside the app are written by Claude Haiku (Anthropic), and we used Claude Code as a coding assistant. There is no hardware and no database. Results are cached by area, period and product.

How it is creative

Many tools of this kind hand you a map and leave the reading to you. We went the other way: the map is only for pointing, and what you get back is a page you can read without training. The site is drawn in pixel art, partly because we like it and partly because a pixel is the honest unit of everything a satellite tells you.

The part we are proudest of is the check on the language model. It never receives the coordinates, only the results the server already computed. Before any text reaches the screen, the server compares every number in it against the report. If the model wrote a figure that is not there, the text is thrown away.

What we considered

The first factor was the problem itself. Before the hackathon we spoke with the president of the Chamber of Farmers of Costa Rica, and he told us this is a very big problem: farmers do not have easy access to this data. That is why we chose it.

The second was not promising more than the data can give. Satellites do not tell you which crop was grown, they do not detect a nematode or a disease, and our soil exposure reading is relative, never tonnes of soil. The app says so on the page. It also never calls a plot good or bad and never recommends a specific crop, because that call belongs to the farmer and the agronomist who know the place.

We also thought about who would use it. The site works in English and Spanish, on a phone, and every number is labelled as observed, modelled, declared by the farmer or taken from a study. The sowing calendars in the rotation step are examples the farmer edits. We could not find a verified calendar for the northern region, so we did not invent one.
